body: Over roughly the next ninety days, these short notes will keep you company as you grow into being a parent while holding on to who you are. Read them whenever you can; there is no wrong time.
Becoming a parent changes almost everything at once. It makes sense if you feel a little lost inside your own life right now.
Exhaustion is real and it is not a failing. Being this tired says something about the work you are doing, not about your worth.
Think of three things you loved doing before the baby arrived. Just name them for now; there is no pressure to do any of them.
Many new parents quietly grieve their old freedom while loving their child fiercely. Both feelings can sit side by side.
Pay attention to how you describe yourself lately. If every sentence starts with the baby, that is understandable, and also worth seeing.
Your identity has not vanished; it has been crowded out by urgent, tiny needs. It is still there underneath.
Look for the parts of your day that belong only to you, even the first sip of tea. Small pockets count.
Comparing yourself with other parents online can sting. Their highlights are not your reality, and your hard moments are not theirs.
Ask yourself what you miss most about your old self. Is it time, spontaneity, conversation, quiet? Naming it helps.
Relationships often shift after a baby. If yours feels strained, that is common, and it does not mean something is broken.
Feeling bored by some baby days does not make you a bad parent. Repetition is hard for any adult brain.
Think about the values you held before becoming a parent. Most of them will still guide you now, perhaps more than ever.
Sleep loss shrinks the world. If everything feels harder than it should, remember that tiredness is colouring the picture.
Watch for the inner critic that says you should be coping better. Answer it as you would answer a worn-out friend.
Some parts of your old life may never return in the same shape. Others are just on pause, waiting for a little space.
If you gave birth, your body may feel unfamiliar for a while. Be patient with it; it has been through a great deal.
Plenty of parents feel they have mislaid their humour, their friendships or their confidence. These things tend to come back in time.
Consider who you can be honest with about how this is going. One true conversation can lift more than you expect.
Letting others help is not a sign of failure. Accepting a meal or an hour of babysitting is part of looking after the whole family.
The person you were before is not gone. They are simply learning to share space with the parent you are becoming.
Find five minutes that are only yours. Sit, breathe, read a page, stare out of the window. It all counts.
Message one friend who knew you before the baby. You do not need a long chat; a simple hello keeps the thread alive.
Put on a song you loved years ago and let yourself enjoy it. Music can return you to yourself surprisingly fast.
Step outside for a short walk, with or without the pram. Fresh air and daylight help on even the foggiest days.
When someone offers help, say yes to one thing this week. Let them hold the baby while you have an uninterrupted shower.
Write down one sentence about how you feel. Keeping a tiny record helps you see how much you are changing.
If the day has been hard, lower the bar. Fed, safe and loved is enough for both of you.
Do one small thing you enjoyed before, even in miniature. Ten minutes of sketching or a chapter of a novel is still you.
Rest when there is a chance, even if the washing can wait. Your energy is a resource worth protecting.
Talk to your partner or a close friend about something that is not the baby. Ordinary conversation helps you reconnect.
Wear something that makes you feel like yourself. A favourite jumper can be a small anchor to who you are.
If you snapped or cried, forgive yourself. Being stretched thin is not the same as failing.
Join a local group, class or walk with other parents. Shared tiredness can turn into real friendship.
Ask for a specific kind of help rather than general support. Clear requests are easier for people to say yes to.
Pick one interest you could take up in a small way this month. A podcast, a craft, an online course you dip in and out of.
Notice moments of joy with your child, however brief. A smile or a sleepy weight on your chest is worth holding on to.
Swap one scroll session for something that restores you. A bath, a stretch, a phone call with someone you love.
If you are sharing the parenting, talk about giving each other regular time off. Taking turns protects you both.
Let some standards slide for now. A tidy house matters far less than a rested parent.
Eat something proper and drink some water. Meeting your own basic needs is part of caring for your child.
Remind yourself of a skill you had before parenthood. Those strengths have not gone; they will be useful again in new ways.
Plan one tiny thing to look forward to this week. Coffee with a friend, a film after bedtime, a slow breakfast.
A bad night does not undo your progress. Start the next day fresh with one small kindness to yourself.
Laugh at the chaos when you can. Finding the funny side is a sign that you are still in there.
Spend a few minutes with an old photograph of yourself. Say hello to that person; they are still part of you.
If you are returning to work, give yourself time to find your feet. Juggling two identities takes practice.
Say no to one thing that drains you. Protecting your energy is not selfish; it is sensible.
Make one decision based on what you need, not only on what the baby needs. Both matter.
When advice comes from every direction, choose what fits your family and let the rest go.
Bring your old interests into family life. Cook the food you love, play your music, take the baby to places you enjoy.
Some days will feel like steps backwards. That is normal, and it does not erase what you have learned.
If low mood or anxiety has lingered for more than a couple of weeks, please talk to your GP or health visitor. Reaching out is a strong and sensible step.
Keep a short list of things that help when you are struggling. On difficult days, you will not have to think, just choose.
Talk with your partner or a friend about who you each want to be as parents. Shared hopes make the load lighter.
Take a photo of something you made or did for yourself this week. Evidence of your own life is worth keeping.
Rest without guilt. A nap is not wasted time; it is care for the person your child depends on.
If you feel isolated, reach out to one person. Connection is often only one message away.
Let yourself be proud of something you managed this week, however small. Getting out of the door counts.
When the baby sleeps, ask yourself what you truly need rather than what you ought to do.
Try a short stretch or some gentle movement for your own sake. Reconnecting with your body can lift your mood.
Speak kindly to yourself out loud once. You would never call a friend useless for being tired, so do not say it to yourself.
If friendships have drifted, pick one and invest a little time. Some of your oldest connections are worth rebuilding.
Think about the example you want to give your child. Seeing you value yourself teaches them to value themselves.
Go somewhere that was yours before the baby: a café, a park, a shop you liked. See how it feels to be there now.
After a tearful week, be gentle with yourself. Feelings move through more easily when they are not fought.
Share a worry with someone you trust. Fears often shrink once they are spoken aloud.
Make a little room for creativity, even scribbles or a few lines in a notebook. Playfulness belongs to you too.
Ask yourself which old habits you want back and which you are happy to leave behind. Growth can mean letting go as well.
Celebrate small milestones of your own, not just the baby's. Your first evening out matters too.
Check in with how you are really doing. Compared with the early weeks, what has eased and what still needs care?
You are becoming someone who can hold both roles: a loving parent and a person with your own needs and interests.
The way you talk about yourself is probably changing. There is more of you in the sentences again.
Parenthood has added new strengths: patience, resilience, an ability to keep going on very little sleep.
You have learned that asking for help is part of being a good parent. That lesson will serve you for years.
Your child is getting to know the real you, not a worn-down outline. That matters more than you might think.
The person you were before has not been replaced. They have grown, and they bring more to the table now.
You are becoming someone who protects small pockets of time for yourself without waiting for permission.
Old friends and new ones are both part of your life now. You are building a circle that fits who you are becoming.
Hard days still come, but you recognise them sooner and recover more kindly. That is real growth.
Consider how you would describe yourself now, beyond the word parent. Let all of those words belong to you.
You have found ways to fold your interests into family life. Your child is growing up around a whole person.
Tiredness may still visit, yet it no longer defines your whole sense of self.
Looking after your own wellbeing has become part of caring for your family, not an afterthought.
Your confidence as a parent has grown alongside your confidence as yourself. Each has fed the other.
Keep making room for the things that make you feel like you. They are part of what you pass on to your child.
You are becoming a parent who is also fully themselves. That balance will keep shifting, and you know how to adjust.
Write a few lines to the version of you who started these notes. Tell them what you now know.
Look back on the early days of fog and doubt. You carried yourself through them, and you are still here.
Some weeks will pull you back towards losing yourself. When that happens, return to one small thing that is yours.
You have grown into being a parent without letting go of who you are. That is no small achievement.
This is the last note in this series. Keep a little time for yourself each day, and let your child see the whole of you.
